name: Akhenaten
info: Akhenaten, born Amenhotep IV, was the 10th ruler of Egypt's 18th Dynasty, reigning c. 1353–1336 or 1351–1334 BCE; he promoted the worship of the Aten, founded the new capital Akhetaten and began the Amarna Period.

facts.born: Probably before his father's 25th regnal year, c. 1363–1361 BCE (Donald Redford's dating; c. 1373 BCE elsewhere), place uncertain (Malkata or Memphis); a younger son of Amenhotep III and Tiye, of the 18th Dynasty
facts.died: In his 17th regnal year, c. 1335 BCE, at Akhetaten (Amarna); first buried in a tomb in the Royal Wadi, then most likely moved to tomb KV55 in the Valley of the Kings, though the identification of the mummy found there remains controversial
facts.role: Pharaoh of Egypt, reigning c. 1353–1336 or 1351–1334 BCE, as Amenhotep IV and from his fifth regnal year as Akhenaten; husband of Nefertiti, his Great Royal Wife
facts.known: promoting the worship of the Aten (Atenism); changing his name from Amenhotep IV; founding the capital Akhetaten (Amarna); the Amarna letters; the naturalistic Amarna art; the later erasure of his name and monuments; the debate over whether Atenism was monotheism

t: Born Amenhotep IV, a younger son who became heir after his brother Thutmose died, he came to the throne c. 1353 or 1351 BCE and in his fifth year took the name Akhenaten, 'Effective for the Aten'.

He founded a new capital at Akhetaten (Amarna), disbanded the priesthoods of the other gods, diverted their income to the Aten and, from about his ninth year, ordered the defacing of Amun's temples throughout Egypt.

After his death his successors dismantled his monuments, destroyed his statues and excluded him from the lists of kings, calling him 'the enemy of Akhetaten'; he was rediscovered only with the late 19th-century finds at Amarna.
dyk: Akhetaten was built so quickly because its builders used small standardised blocks called talatats, about 27 by 27 by 54 cm; when archaeologists later dismantled the infill of Karnak's pylons, some 36,000 decorated blocks from his Theban Aten temples emerged.
ev: Amenhotep IV is born, according to Donald Redford's dating, a younger son of Amenhotep III and Tiye
He takes the throne as Amenhotep IV, in 1353 or 1351 BCE, most likely crowned at Thebes, and begins temples to the Aten at Karnak and elsewhere
In his second regnal year he gives a speech, preserved on a pylon at Karnak, saying that the gods had ceased their appearances except the god who gave birth to himself
In his fifth regnal year he changes his name to Akhenaten and decrees a new capital, Akhetaten, now called Amarna
In about his ninth regnal year he declares the Aten the only worshipable god and orders the defacing of Amun's temples throughout Egypt
In his twelfth regnal year the royal family receives tribute from Nubia, Punt, Syria, the Mediterranean islands and Libya at Akhetaten
Akhenaten dies and is buried in a tomb in the Royal Wadi east of Akhetaten
Tutankhaten changes his name to Tutankhamun and abandons Akhetaten, and Egypt returns gradually to its traditional religion

sections.early:
Akhenaten was born Amenhotep IV, a younger son of the pharaoh Amenhotep III and his principal wife, Tiye. He had an elder brother, crown prince Thutmose, who was recognised as heir, and four or five sisters: Sitamun, Henuttaneb, Iset, Nebetah and possibly Beketaten. Egyptologists know very little of his life as a prince. Donald Redford dates his birth before his father's 25th regnal year, c. 1363–1361 BCE, from the birth of his first daughter, who was likely born fairly early in his reign. The only mention of his name, as "the King's Son Amenhotep", was found on a wine docket at Amenhotep III's Malkata palace, where some historians suggested he was born; others contend he was born in Memphis.

Thutmose's early death, perhaps around Amenhotep III's 30th regnal year, made Amenhotep IV next in line. Historians have proposed several tutors, among them the scribes Heqareshu or Meryre II, the royal tutor Amenemotep and the vizier Aperel; the only person known for certain to have served the prince is Parennefer, whose tomb mentions it. Cyril Aldred suggested that he might have been High Priest of Ptah in Memphis, as Thutmose had been, although no evidence for this has been found. Redford and James Hoffmeier note that the cult of Ra was so widespread in Egypt that he could have been influenced by solar worship wherever he grew up.
sections.rise:
Scholars disagree about how he came to the throne. Eric Cline, Nicholas Reeves, Peter Dorman and others argue against a long coregency with Amenhotep III, favouring none or one lasting at most two years, while Donald Redford, William Murnane, Alan Gardiner and Lawrence Berman reject any coregency. In 2014 archaeologists found both pharaohs' names in the Luxor tomb of the vizier Amenhotep-Huy, which Egypt's Ministry of Antiquities called conclusive evidence of at least eight years of shared power; other Egyptologists say it shows only that the tomb was begun under one king and finished under the other.

Amenhotep IV took the throne most likely in 1353 or 1351 BCE; estimates of his age at accession range from 10 to 23. His reign began in the established manner. Inscriptions show him worshipping several gods, the High Priest of Amun was still active in his fourth year, and he continued his father's building at Karnak's Precinct of Amun-Re. At the same time he built shrines to the Aten in cities including Bubastis, Heliopolis, Memphis and Kawa, and a large temple complex, the Per Aten, at Karnak. Around his second or third year he held a Sed festival, a rite usually held about the thirtieth year of a reign. Egyptologists only speculate why; they believe he made offerings during it to the Aten alone. He married Nefertiti, his Great Royal Wife, either shortly before or after taking the throne.
sections.deeds:
In his fifth regnal year Amenhotep IV took decisive steps to establish the Aten as the sole god of Egypt: he disbanded the priesthoods of the other gods, diverted their income to the Aten and changed his name to Akhenaten, understood by Gertie Englund and Florence Friedman as "Effective for the Aten". About the same time he decreed a new capital, Akhetaten, on an uninhabited site on the east bank of the Nile about halfway between Thebes and Memphis. Its boundary stelae survive. It was built quickly with small talatat blocks, and by his eighth year the royal family could live there; only his most loyal subjects followed. By his ninth year he declared the Aten the only worshipable god, ordered Amun's temples defaced throughout Egypt, and banned images other than a rayed solar disc.

The Great Hymn to the Aten, found in the tomb of Ay, may have been composed by Akhenaten himself. It calls the Aten a sole god and creator and names the king as the only one who knows him. In foreign affairs the 382 Amarna letters show a pharaoh who kept control of the core of Egypt's Near Eastern empire, while avoiding conflict with the Hittites. Only one campaign is known for certain, against Nubian nomads in his second or twelfth year; Wolfgang Helck called it a small police operation and Alan Schulman a war of major proportions.
sections.opponents:
The boundary stela that explained the move to Akhetaten is damaged, but its surviving parts speak of something worse than the king had heard before and of speech offensive to the Aten. Egyptologists believe this refers to conflict with the priesthood and followers of Amun; Donald Redford suggested he was trying to break with them. Evidence on how far he forced his reforms is mixed. Some courtiers kept names such as Ahmose, and a sculptor at Amarna was called Thutmose, after Thoth; amulets of Bes, Taweret and the eye of Horus were openly worn there. Yet ordinary residents also chiselled out references to Amun on small personal items, perhaps for fear of being accused of Amunist sympathies. His policies may have been fairly tolerant until some point toward the end of the reign.

His vassal Rib-Hadda of Byblos wrote 60 letters pleading for help against Amurru, and Akhenaten did not send an army; Rib-Hadda was exiled and almost certainly executed. Early Egyptologists such as Henry Hall and James Henry Breasted read the letters as showing a pacifist who neglected foreign policy, a view discounted by the 21st century. Jacobus van Dijk and Jan Assmann hold that the Amarna period began a gradual decline in the pharaoh's standing, because the reforms subverted how ordinary Egyptians related to their gods and king.
sections.last:
The last five years of the reign are poorly attested. The year 12 reception, at which the royal family received tribute from Nubia, Punt, Syria, the Mediterranean islands and Libya, is regarded by Aidan Dodson as the zenith of the reign. Donald Redford and others proposed that an epidemic, most likely plague, struck Egypt afterwards; it might account for the deaths of his daughters Meketaten, Neferneferure and Setepenre. An inscription found in 2012 at Deir el-Bersha, dated to year 16, shows that Akhenaten and Nefertiti were still a royal couple a year before his death. He may have ruled with Smenkhkare, who could have been his coregent by year 13 or 14, and later with Nefertiti.

Akhenaten died in his 17th year and was first buried in a tomb in the Royal Wadi east of Akhetaten, which he had ordered on a boundary stela. His mummy was removed after Tutankhaten left Akhetaten and was most likely moved to tomb KV55 near Thebes, later desecrated. Whether the mummy found there in 1907 is his remains controversial: a team led by Zahi Hawass in 2010 called it the father of Tutankhamun and thus most probably Akhenaten, but others, among them Juan Belmonte, consider it more likely to be Smenkhkare. Smenkhkare may have ruled briefly alone; some think Nefertiti or Meritaten then ruled as Neferneferuaten for about two years, followed by Tutankhaten, with the vizier Ay administering the country.
sections.legacy:
After his death the Aten cult fell out of favour, at first gradually and then decisively. Tutankhaten changed his name to Tutankhamun in the second year of his reign, c. 1332 BCE, and abandoned Akhetaten. Under Horemheb, the first pharaoh after Akhenaten who was not related to his family, temples to the Aten were destroyed and their blocks reused, including for temples of the restored Amun. Seti I restored Amun's name on inscriptions and had Akhenaten, Smenkhkare, Neferneferuaten, Tutankhamun and Ay excised from the lists of pharaohs. The Ramessides gradually destroyed Akhetaten. Later records call him "the enemy of Akhetaten" or "that criminal". The reforms also left a mark on language: texts of the Amarna period included more vernacular forms, which remained common in official texts from the 19th Dynasty.

Akhenaten was all but lost to history until the late 19th-century discovery of Amarna. Whether Atenism was monotheism is disputed: some Egyptologists call it monolatrous, syncretistic or henotheistic, since he did not deny other gods. Sigmund Freud argued that Moses had been an Atenist priest; in 1997 Redford concluded there is little or no evidence that Akhenaten was a progenitor of the monotheism of the Bible, which had its own development beginning more than half a millennium after his death. Scholars such as Brian Fagan and Robert Alter have since reopened the debate. He has been described from "the first individual in history" to "heretic" and "possibly insane". The Druze faith recognises him as a prophet.

summary: Akhenaten (born Amenhotep IV, reigned c. 1353–1336 or 1351–1334 BCE) elevated the Aten above Egypt's other gods, founded Akhetaten (Amarna) and changed his name in his fifth year. His successors erased his monuments and name; scholars still dispute whether Atenism was monotheism.
references: Cyril Aldred, Akhenaten, Pharaoh of Egypt: A New Study (Thames and Hudson, 1968)
Cyril Aldred, Akhenaten, King of Egypt (Thames and Hudson, 1991)
Aidan Dodson, Amarna Sunrise: Egypt from the Golden Age to Age of Heresy (The American University in Cairo Press, 2014)
notes: Birth: the lead gives c. 1373 BC, but the body gives Redford's c. 1363–1361 BC from the birth of his first daughter; start -1363 with circa true, and the 'born' fact gives both. Death: the lead gives c. 1335 BC; reign dates given as 1353–1336 or 1351–1334 BC, so end -1335 with endCirca true.

Regnal-year event labels (Year 2, 5, 9, 12, 17) are used because the article dates these events by regnal year only; the editor may convert them. The year-5 name change and the year-5 'decisive steps' are dated by the article to Year Five. The article also says the Aten's priesthoods were disbanded in year 5 and that the defacing of Amun's temples began by year 9.
Nubian campaign: article says 'second or 12th year'; both given. Sed festival 'around regnal year two or three'.
Coregency with Amenhotep III is disputed; presented as disputed. Smenkhkare's identity and the KV55 mummy's identity are disputed; told as such.

The article contradicts itself on when work stopped at Amarna: 'abandoned Amarna Tutankhaten around 3 years after Akhenaten's death' (garbled) while the legacy section says Tutankhaten changed name in his Year 2 (c. 1332 BC); I used c. 1332 BCE for the abandonment/return to Thebes only as the article's date for the name change, and left out the three-year claim.

Left out: paternity of Tutankhamun and the debate over marriages to his daughters (sensitive and heavily disputed; not needed for the life); illness theories; cultural depictions (films, opera, games, songs); Nefertiti's role in art. The article's phrase on the Druze faith is in legacy.
'Decisive steps to establish the Aten as the sole god' is quoted-style wording of the article; the 'disbanded priesthoods' claim comes from a quoted source inside the article.
The 'rise' section says marriage 'either shortly before or after taking the throne' per the article; Laboury's suggestion of regnal year four was left out.

The article's phrase 'Egyptologists know little' appears in the last section; this is the article's own hedge. Garbled sentence about Tutankhaten and the 'Royal tomb' abandonment left out. Sarcophagus detail left out.
